items.followUp: What is the difference between taxonomy and systematics?

rubric.why: Taxonomy aims to identify, name and classify organisms.
rubric.description: States an aim of taxonomy, such as identifying, naming or classifying organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one of these aims.

rubric.why: Systematics studies the diversity of organisms and their relationships, including evolutionary relationships.
rubric.description: States that systematics studies organismal diversity or relationships.

modelAnswer: Taxonomy aims to identify, name and classify organisms.
Systematics studies the diversity of organisms and their relationships, including their evolutionary relationships.

items.followUp: How do benign tumours differ from malignant tumours?

rubric.why: A benign tumour remains at its original site.
rubric.description: States that a benign tumour remains localized or confined to its original site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying that it stays at its original location.

rubric.why: Benign tumours do not invade nearby tissues or spread to other parts of the body.
rubric.description: States that a benign tumour does not invade or spread to other tissues or body parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it does not invade or spread.

modelAnswer: A benign tumour is an abnormal mass of cells that remains localized at its original site.
It does not invade nearby tissues or spread to other parts of the body.

items.followUp: What happens to an enzyme's active site when the enzyme is denatured?

rubric.why: Denaturation changes the enzyme's shape, including the shape of its active site.
rubric.description: States that denaturation changes the enzyme's shape or active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the structural change.

rubric.why: The altered shape prevents normal substrate binding and the enzyme loses its catalytic function.
rubric.description: States that the enzyme loses activity or can no longer bind its substrate properly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the resulting loss of function.

modelAnswer: Denaturation is a change in an enzyme's three-dimensional shape, including the shape of its active site.
The substrate can no longer bind properly, so the enzyme loses its catalytic activity.
